question: How many U.S. Coast Guard-approved wearable personal flotation devices (PFDs) must a recreational vessel in New York carry?
choice_a: At least one properly sized, USCG-approved wearable PFD for every person on board
choice_b: Only one PFD total regardless of how many people are aboard
choice_c: PFDs are optional if the boat has a radio
choice_d: Two PFDs, regardless of the number of occupants
explanation: New York law, like federal law, requires one wearable, properly fitted, USCG-approved PFD for each person aboard the vessel, in serviceable condition and readily accessible.
source_note: NY Navigation Law / parks.ny.gov PFD Laws of New York

question: Under New York's child life-jacket law, which children must actually wear (not just have available) a PFD on a vessel 65 feet or less while underway?
choice_b: Children under 12 years of age, unless they are within a fully enclosed cabin
choice_c: No age group is required to wear a PFD in New York
choice_d: Only children who cannot swim, regardless of age
explanation: New York requires every child under 12 aboard a vessel 65 feet or less to wear a USCG-approved Type I, II, or III PFD while underway, except when inside a fully enclosed cabin.
source_note: parks.ny.gov PFD Laws of New York, child PFD requirement

question: During what period of the year does New York require everyone aboard a vessel less than 21 feet long to wear a PFD while underway, regardless of age?
choice_d: New York has no seasonal PFD-wear requirement
explanation: New York's cold-weather PFD law requires all occupants of vessels under 21 feet -- including kayaks, canoes, and rowboats -- to wear a life jacket while underway from November 1 through May 1.
source_note: NY Navigation Law seasonal PFD requirement, parks.ny.gov / Waterway Guide coverage

question: What must every operator and passenger on a personal watercraft (PWC) in New York wear at all times while the PWC is underway?
choice_a: Nothing is required as long as the PWC has a kill switch
choice_b: A PFD only if operating after sunset
choice_c: A wetsuit, which legally substitutes for a PFD
choice_d: A properly fitted, USCG-approved wearable PFD
explanation: New York law requires every person on a PWC, operator and passengers alike, to wear a USCG-approved wearable PFD at all times the PWC is in operation -- a wetsuit does not satisfy this requirement.
source_note: NY Navigation Law PWC requirements, parks.ny.gov Personal Watercraft page

question: What is the key difference between a Type I and a Type III PFD?
choice_a: A Type I offshore life jacket is designed to turn most unconscious wearers face-up and provides the most buoyancy, while a Type III flotation aid is more comfortable for continuous wear but may not turn an unconscious person face-up
choice_b: A Type III provides more buoyancy than a Type I
choice_c: Type I and Type III are identical in design and purpose
choice_d: A Type III is only for use on PWCs
explanation: Type I offshore life jackets offer the highest buoyancy and reliably turn most unconscious wearers face-up in open, rough water, while Type III flotation aids are more comfortable for continuous wear in calmer, closer-to-shore conditions but offer less turning ability.
source_note: USCG PFD type classifications, standard NASBLA-course content

question: What is a Type IV PFD, and what New York vessels are required to carry one in addition to wearable PFDs?
choice_a: A wearable jacket required only for children
choice_b: A throwable device such as a ring buoy or buoyant cushion, required on vessels 16 feet and longer (except canoes and kayaks) in addition to wearable PFDs for each person aboard
choice_c: A type of PFD that is inflated only by mouth and never carried on recreational boats
choice_d: A device required only on PWCs
explanation: A Type IV throwable device (ring buoy or buoyant cushion) must be immediately available for quick use aboard vessels 16 feet or longer, in addition to a wearable PFD for each person; canoes and kayaks are exempt from the throwable requirement.
source_note: parks.ny.gov PFD Laws of New York, throwable device requirement

question: Is an inflatable PFD an appropriate choice for a child under 16 in New York?
choice_a: Yes, inflatable PFDs are the only approved option for children
choice_b: Yes, but only in salt water
choice_c: No, inflatable PFDs are not approved for use by persons under 16 years of age
choice_d: Inflatable PFDs have no age restriction
explanation: Inflatable PFDs require the wearer to be able to activate or otherwise rely on inflation and are not USCG-approved for use by persons under age 16; a properly sized inherently buoyant Type I, II, or III should be used instead.
source_note: USCG inflatable PFD age restriction, standard NASBLA-course content

question: For a PFD to count as 'properly worn' under New York's regulations, what must be true of its straps and zippers?
choice_a: Straps only matter for adults, not children
choice_b: PFDs never have straps or zippers that need fastening
choice_c: It is acceptable to wear a PFD unfastened as long as it is on the body
choice_d: All straps and/or zippers must be fastened, tied, or zipped as designed, not left loose or undone
explanation: New York's PFD-law guidance specifies that a device is only considered properly worn when all its straps and/or zippers are secured; an unfastened PFD can slip off in the water and fail to perform.
source_note: parks.ny.gov PFD Laws of New York, proper-wear guidance

question: What condition must a PFD be in to satisfy New York's carriage requirement?
choice_a: It must be in good, serviceable condition, of the appropriate size for the intended wearer, and readily accessible
choice_b: Condition does not matter as long as it is on board somewhere
choice_c: It only needs to float, regardless of fit or wear
choice_d: It must be brand new each boating season
explanation: A PFD that is torn, waterlogged, missing straps, or the wrong size for its intended wearer does not satisfy the legal carriage requirement -- it must be serviceable, properly sized, and readily accessible.
source_note: USCG/NY PFD serviceability standards, standard NASBLA-course content

question: A water skier or person being towed behind a boat in New York must:
choice_a: Have a PFD stored in the towing boat but need not wear it
choice_b: Wear a USCG-approved PFD, not merely have one available in the boat
choice_c: Wear a PFD only if under age 12
choice_d: Never wear a PFD, since it could interfere with skiing
explanation: Anyone being towed on water skis, a tube, or similar equipment must actually wear a PFD; simply having one stowed in the tow boat is not sufficient.
source_note: NY Navigation Law towed-person requirements, water sports

question: What is a Type V PFD?
choice_a: A device approved for any use with no restrictions
choice_b: The most basic and least protective PFD category
choice_c: A special-use device (such as a deck suit, work vest, or hybrid inflatable) that is only USCG-approved when used according to the conditions on its label, such as a specific activity
choice_d: A device intended exclusively for pets
explanation: Type V PFDs are special-use devices that only meet approval requirements when used for the specific activity and conditions stated on the label -- otherwise they may not provide the intended protection.
source_note: USCG PFD type classifications, standard NASBLA-course content

question: Why do NASBLA-approved courses emphasize wearing a PFD at all times on the water rather than just having one on board?
choice_a: PFDs are only useful for people who cannot swim
choice_b: Wearing a PFD is required only for demonstration purposes during a safety inspection
choice_c: PFDs are uncomfortable and should be avoided unless legally mandated every second
choice_d: Most boating fatalities are drownings, and a PFD only works if it is being worn when an unexpected fall overboard or capsizing occurs -- there is rarely time to put one on once you're in the water
explanation: The majority of boating drowning victims were not wearing a PFD; falls overboard and capsizings often happen suddenly, leaving no time to retrieve and don a stowed life jacket.
source_note: USCG boating fatality statistics, standard NASBLA-course content

question: Cold water significantly changes how effective a PFD needs to be. Why is this especially relevant for boaters on New York's northern lakes and Great Lakes waters?
choice_a: Cold water accelerates the onset of incapacitation and hypothermia, so a worn PFD that keeps a person's airway above water is critical for survival until rescue, even for strong swimmers
choice_b: Cold water makes PFDs float better and is otherwise not a safety concern
choice_c: PFDs are not needed in cold water because cold water increases natural buoyancy
choice_d: Cold water only affects PWC operators, not other boaters
explanation: Cold water causes rapid loss of muscle control and can incapacitate even strong swimmers within minutes; a worn PFD keeps a person's head and airway above water while they wait for rescue or attempt self-rescue.
source_note: Cold-water immersion physiology, relevant to NY's Great Lakes/northern climate, standard NASBLA-course content
